1.synthesis:
The Ṛgveda opens with fire, and with a job description. Agni is invoked as the *purohita* of the sacrifice — the priest placed in front, the one who superintends the household rite — and as the *hotā*, the one who calls the gods to the offering and carries the oblation up to them. Both roles are about movement between two worlds. Agni is the only god who is physically present on the ground, burning in the hearth, and the whole logic of the offering depends on him: what is poured into the fire is what reaches the gods. Sāyaṇa reads the opening word as pointing to that office directly, and derives it from the fire in which oblations are placed *first*.

The sūkta then makes a claim about continuity. Agni is worthy to be praised by the ancient seers and by the present ones alike — the same fire, the same address, across generations, which is a statement about the tradition's own transmission as much as about the god. From that follow the practical goods: wealth that increases day by day, abundance in offspring and heroes, and the assurance that a sacrifice Agni encircles reaches the gods unobstructed. Sāyaṇa notes that the fires stand at the cardinal points of the ritual ground, so "encompassing on every side" is a description of the physical altar, not a figure of speech.

What lifts the sūkta above ritual bookkeeping is where it ends. After eight verses of office and function, the ninth drops all of it: *be easy of access to us, as a father to his son; be ever present with us for our good.* The collection opens by asking the fire that mediates everything to be, first of all, approachable.
1.disagreements:
Wilson and Griffith split on the opening line and the split runs through. Wilson has "the high priest of the sacrifice, the divine, the ministrant" — offices, following Sāyaṇa's gloss of *purohita* as the priest of family rites. Griffith gives "the chosen Priest, God, minister of sacrifice, The hotar," leaving *hotā* untranslated and adding "lavishest of wealth," which reads as praise rather than function.

Verse 6 is the sharper case. Wilson has Agni's gift "revert to you, Aṅgiras" — a name Sāyaṇa connects to *aṅgāra*, a live coal, citing the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa that the coals became the Aṅgirasas. Griffith's "That, Angiras, is indeed thy truth" preserves the vocative but drops the identification, so the reader cannot see why a fire is being addressed by a seer's name.

2.synthesis:
A soma sūkta, and a guest list. The pressed juice has been prepared and the priest calls its drinkers in order: Vāyu alone for three verses, Indra together with Vāyu for three, then Mitra with Varuṇa for the last three. The structure is the content — this is what an invitation to a shared offering looks like when it is formalised, and the triadic shape recurs across the early collection.

Vāyu, the wind, is addressed as one who comes to look upon the offering and to hear the call. Wilson's reading, following Sāyaṇa, makes the exchange explicitly verbal: Vāyu's approving speech goes out to the giver, and Sāyaṇa supplies the god's own words — *I will drink the libation*. The invitation is answered. When Indra joins him the register shifts to speed and appetite; the drops themselves are described as yearning for the two gods, which inverts the usual direction of desire in a ritual.

The final triad carries the weight. Mitra and Varuṇa are invoked as the pair who preside over the daylit and the nocturnal order — Sāyaṇa identifies Mitra with the sun and Varuṇa with the waters, both among the Ādityas — and they are called *ṛtāvṛdhau*, those who grow by ṛta and make it grow. Wilson renders them augmenters and dispensers of water who connect the rite to its true reward, and Sāyaṇa observes that *ṛta* carries truth, water, and sacrifice in one word. That triple sense is the reason the pair can be addressed as cosmic and meteorological at once, and it is the sūkta's most important idea.
2.disagreements:
The *ṛta* verses are where the two translators visibly part. Wilson keeps the concrete senses — "augmenters of water, dispensers of water" — because Sāyaṇa lets the word mean water and sacrifice as well as truth. Griffith goes straight to abstraction: "through Law, lovers and cherishers of Law." One reading has gods who make the rains work; the other has gods who uphold a principle.

Verse 3 divides the same way. Wilson's Vāyu answers with "approving speech"; Griffith's Vāyu sends "thy penetrating stream" toward the worshipper. In one the god replies, in the other the weather arrives.

3.synthesis:
Twelve verses moving through four addresses in threes: the Aśvins, Indra, the Viśvedevas, and Sarasvatī. Like the two sūktas before it this is an invitation sequence, but the guests are more varied and the closing triad opens onto something much larger than the rite.

The Aśvins come first — twin horsemen, called here nimble-handed and rich, urged to accept the offering with outstretched hands. Sāyaṇa records the tradition that they are the physicians of the gods, and glosses their epithet *rudravartani* as those who travel in the van of heroes, deriving *rudra* from the root for weeping: those who make their enemies weep. Indra follows, drawn by tawny horses, and the soma is described as purified by the priests' own fingers — the ritual detail is precise. The Viśvedevas, the All-Gods taken as a class, arrive next; they are asked to come as swiftly as the sun's rays come to the day.

Then Sarasvatī, and the sūkta changes scale. She is invoked as purifier, as the one who rewards worship with abundance, and as the inspirer of those who delight in truth and the instructor of the right-minded. The final verse holds her two aspects together without resolving them: she makes manifest a mighty river, and she illuminates all understandings. Sāyaṇa states the doubling outright, citing the Nirukta that Sarasvatī is twofold — an embodied deity and a river — and that the hymns speak of her in both ways. She is the earliest and clearest instance in the collection of a power that is simultaneously a place on the map and a faculty of mind.
3.disagreements:
Sarasvatī is where the readings diverge most consequentially. Wilson's verse 12 keeps both aspects as genuinely two — she manifests a river *and*, in her own form, enlightens the understanding — which is what Sāyaṇa's twofold gloss requires. Griffith compresses to "the mighty flood — she with her light illuminates, She brightens every pious thought," which reads as metaphor: a river used to describe a mind. The tradition treats the duality as real; the Victorian translation resolves it into figure.

Verse 9 divides on a single epithet. Wilson has the Viśvedevas "exempt from decay, omniscient, devoid of malice"; Griffith has them "changing shape like serpents, fearless, void of guile." The same word is read as universal knowledge or as serpentine shape-shifting.
